title: Koreans Track a Fish-Shaped Snack on a Map

slides.headline: Koreans track this fish-shaped snack **on a map.**
slides.note: And it only shows up when it gets cold.

slides.headline: It's called **bungeoppang**
slides.body: Bungeoppang (붕어빵) means "carp bread". Crispy fish-shaped batter, sweet red bean inside. No fish anywhere.

slides.headline: Borrowed, **then made Korean**
slides.body: It traces back to Japan's taiyaki. Decades on the street turned it into Korea's own winter snack.

slides.headline: Only when **the cold comes**
slides.body: Stalls pop up when the wind turns cold and vanish by spring. The first one you spot means winter is here.

slides.headline: Living near one **has a name**
slides.body: Near a subway station is yeoksekwon (역세권). Near a bungeoppang stall? Bungsekwon (붕세권).

slides.headline: No address. **So people map them.**
slides.body: Stalls move and have no sign online, so Koreans pin them on street-snack map apps and share the spots.

slides.headline: Head or tail **first?**
slides.body: Koreans genuinely argue about which end to bite first. Red bean versus custard is the other fight.

slides.headline: Once bought **three**
slides.body: A ₩1,000 bill used to get you three. Now it often buys one, two at best.

slides.headline: Not just a snack. **A winter signal.**
slides.body: In Korea, winter starts the day the first stall opens on your street.

slides.headline: Korea, explained **by a Korean.**
slides.body: Follow for the context behind the things Korea does.
slides.graphic: A Seoul street at dusk with a small glowing snack stall, softly blurred behind the text.

caption:
Korea's favorite winter street snack is a fish-shaped bread with red bean inside, and Koreans literally pin the stalls on a map.

It's called bungeoppang. The stalls only appear when it gets cold, and living near one even has its own word.

Head or tail first?
reply: One more: there's a near-twin called ingeoppang, named after a different kind of carp, with thinner and crispier batter. Most people can't tell which one they're eating. What street snack tells you winter has arrived where you live?
fact_check: 3장: 일본 다이야키 기원설이 일반적(일제강점기 전래, 전후 대중화). 연도 단정 피함.
5장: 붕세권=역세권 패러디 신조어, 언론 다수 사용.
6장: '가슴속 3천원' 등 노점 지도 앱 존재. 앱 이름 안 씀.
댓글: 잉어빵=잉어(carp), 붕어빵=붕어(crucian carp). 반죽 얇고 바삭하다는 설명이 일반적.
